content: The references provided are a collection of studies, reviews, and guidelines related to cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk assessment, prevention, and management in various populations, including those living with HIV, as well as broader public health interventions for non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and mental health. 1. Willis et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review to evaluate the use of validated risk scores for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease. The study emphasized the importance of accurate risk stratification tools in clinical practice to guide preventive interventions. 2. Friis-Møller and Worm (2007) explored whether conventional cardiovascular risk prediction tools are applicable to HIV-infected patients. Their findings highlighted the limitations of traditional models in this unique population, necessitating tailored approaches. 3. Knobel et al. (2007) compared global cardiovascular risk estimates in HIV-infected patients using three different risk equations: Framingham, SCORE, and PROCAM. The study revealed discrepancies in risk predictions, underscoring the need for population-specific models. 4. Parra et al. (2010) investigated the lack of concordance between subclinical atherosclerosis and the Framingham risk score in HIV-infected patients. They examined the relationships between oxidative stress, inflammation markers, and cardiovascular risk, suggesting that traditional risk scores may underestimate risk in this group. 5. Pirs et al. (2014) compared cardiovascular risk assessment models, including Framingham, SCORE, PROCAM, and DAD, in HIV-infected male patients. The study provided insights into the relative performance of these models in predicting cardiovascular events. 6. Regan et al. (2015) evaluated the ACC/AHA cardiovascular disease risk prediction algorithm in HIV-infected patients. This study, presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI), highlighted the need for further validation of this tool in HIV populations. 7. Thompson-Paul et al. (2015) assessed cardiovascular disease risk prediction in the HIV Outpatient Study (HOPS). Their findings, also presented at CROI, contributed to understanding the applicability of existing risk models in clinical care for HIV patients. 8. Markowicz et al. (2014) conducted a case-control study comparing the DAD and Framingham equations for cardiovascular risk evaluation in HIV-positive patients. The study demonstrated the higher accuracy of the DAD model in this population. 9. Begovac et al. (2015) compared four international cardiovascular disease prediction models and assessed the prevalence of eligibility for lipid-lowering therapy in HIV-infected patients on antiretroviral therapy. The study highlighted the variability in treatment recommendations based on the model used. 10. Friis-Møller et al. (2010) developed a cardiovascular risk prediction model specifically for HIV-infected patients as part of the DAD study. This model incorporated HIV-specific factors to improve risk stratification. 11. Friis-Møller et al. (2016) updated the DAD risk prediction model to reflect the global cardiovascular risk in HIV-positive individuals. The revised model aimed to enhance clinical decision-making for this population. 12. Serrano-Villar et al. (2014) demonstrated that the DAD risk equation outperformed the Framingham and SCORE algorithms in diagnosing subclinical atherosclerosis in HIV-infected patients. This study emphasized the importance of using HIV-specific tools for cardiovascular risk assessment. 13. Wangchuk et al. (2014) assessed the implementation of the WHO Package of Essential Non-Communicable Disease (PEN) interventions in primary healthcare settings in Bhutan. The study evaluated the performance and feasibility of integrating NCD care into resource-limited settings. 14. Zou et al. (2015) examined the use of medications and lifestyle modifications among hypertensive patients at high risk of cardiovascular disease in rural China. The study highlighted gaps in adherence to recommended interventions. 15. Wei et al. (2013) conducted a clustered randomized controlled trial in rural China to evaluate strategies for reducing cardiovascular disease risk. The trial provided evidence for the effectiveness of community-based interventions. 16. Burkholder et al. (2012) reported on the underutilization of aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease among HIV-infected patients. The study called for increased awareness and implementation of preventive measures in this population. 17. Suchindran et al. (2014) compared aspirin use for primary and secondary prevention in HIV-infected and uninfected patients. The findings underscored the need for targeted strategies to address disparities in preventive care. 18. Pearce et al. (2012) compared in-hospital mortality rates from acute myocardial infarction between HIV-positive and HIV-negative individuals. The study highlighted the increased cardiovascular risk associated with HIV infection. 19. Feinstein et al. (2015) conducted a systematic review on the utility of statin therapy in HIV-infected patients. The review supported the use of statins for managing dyslipidemia and reducing cardiovascular risk in this population. 20. Tiam et al. (2012) described an innovative approach to providing integrated health services for HIV and non-communicable diseases in hard-to-reach areas of Lesotho. The study emphasized the importance of family health days in improving access to care. 21. Kotwani et al. (2014) evaluated linkage to care for hypertension following community-based screening in rural Uganda. The study identified barriers and facilitators to effective care integration. 22. Cook et al. (2004) examined the relationship between depressive symptoms and AIDS-related mortality among HIV-positive women. The study highlighted the critical role of mental health in improving outcomes for people living with HIV. 23. Sin and DiMatteo (2014) conducted a meta-analysis demonstrating that depression treatment enhances adherence to antiretroviral therapy. The findings supported the integration of mental health services into HIV care. 24. Nakimuli-Mpungu et al. (2012) reviewed the impact of depression and alcohol use on adherence to antiretroviral therapy in sub-Saharan Africa. The study emphasized the need for comprehensive care addressing mental health and substance use. 25. Springer et al. (2012) systematically reviewed the impact of DSM-IV mental disorders on adherence to combination antiretroviral therapy. The findings underscored the importance of addressing mental health to optimize HIV treatment outcomes. 26. WHO guidelines (2013) provided operational recommendations for implementing antiretroviral therapy in resource-limited settings. The guidelines emphasized differentiated care, task shifting, and community-based delivery models to improve service quality and efficiency. 27. The WHO Mental Health Action Plan (2013–2020) outlined strategies for integrating mental health services into primary care, particularly in low-resource settings. The plan aimed to close treatment gaps and improve outcomes for people with mental health disorders. These studies and guidelines collectively highlight the importance of tailored approaches to cardiovascular risk assessment, mental health integration, and service delivery in diverse populations, particularly those living with HIV or in resource-limited settings.
